items.quote: The Duty of Natures Minister, the Physitian.
items.what: The Duty of Natures Minister, the Physitian
items.note: Chapter heading: the chapter is set apart as about the physician's duty, the physician being named Nature's minister.

items.name: P. Ramus
items.quote: ALL common Philosophy was not bound up in Aaistotle, as P. Ramus hath soundly proved
items.note: Croll leans on Ramus for the claim that philosophy is not confined to Aristotle.

items.quote: nor was the whole Light of Nature drawne into Galen and limited in him only, witnesse Paracelsus
items.note: Croll holds that the Light of Nature is not confined to Galen, citing Paracelsus as evidence.

items.quote: No man ought to deprive another of the liberty of human ingenuity, that Light of Nature, the power to discern and judge as well as himselfe
items.note: Here the Light of Nature is put in apposition with human ingenuity and the power to discern and judge; each person has a right to it.

items.quote: he that would be an Excellent Physitian he must be free from every kind of Sect.
items.note: The excellent physician must be bound to no sect or single author.

items.quote: to follow the naked Truth, and subscribe to it alone
items.note: The physician is to follow truth alone, not an author's opinion.

items.name: Horace
items.quote: I think and judge as cause I finde
items.note: Verse introduced in CH5.1 as 'that of Horace': judging by reasons found, not by another's mind.

items.name: Horace
items.quote: Nutlius addictus jurare in verba magistri.
items.note: The margin gives the Latin lines beside the English verse of CH5.2, the source of the Horace quotation.

items.quote: all sects, be they never so many, may well be admitted, because in every one of them there is some thing excellent which is not common to another
items.note: Croll qualifies CH5.1: other sects are not to be slighted, since each has something excellent of its own.

items.name: Picus Mirandula
items.quote: as said that most noble and wise Picus Mirandula the Phaenix of Phylosophers
items.note: The view that every sect has something excellent is attributed to Picus Mirandula, praised at length.

items.quote: There is no book so base and bad but hath some good in it
items.note: Even bad books hold some good that the best authors have missed.

items.name: Fabius
items.quote: This latter age, saith Fabius, hath endeavored to make the former more compleat
items.note: Fabius is cited for the later age completing the former.

items.quote: many loathsome errours of the Heathen have been as by a second song
items.note: Errors of the Heathen have been wiped away by later, wiser men; 'as by a second song' is a figure for that correction.

items.quote: All Secret are by divine Ordination to be discovered.
items.note: The margin states that every secret is ordained by God to be uncovered in time.

items.quote: Doubtlesse there are more secrets yet concealed in the Treasures of Wisdome and Nature then we perceive
items.note: Secrets still lie concealed in wisdom and nature.

items.quote: being ordained for Times and Nations, by an immutable decree, to the end of the world) are to be sought out by wise-hearted men
items.note: These hidden secrets are assigned by decree to times and nations and are to be sought out by the wise-hearted.

items.quote: Nature certainly, being Circularly, can hardly be wholly comprehended by any mortall man by reason of the shortnesse of his life.
items.note: Nature, being 'Circularly', cannot be wholly grasped in one short life; the sense of 'Circularly' is not explained in these lines.

items.quote: neither the Physick of the Ancients, nor that of Theophrastus, is totally to be rejected
items.note: Neither ancient physic nor that of Theophrastus is to be wholly rejected; better findings are to be received and the best of both kept.

items.quote: both should be compared together, what is best in both let that be cetained
items.note: A method of comparison: keep what is best in both.

items.quote: reserving many things to himselfe that we might alway acknowledge him to be our only teacher
items.note: The holy Spirit withholds many things so that he remains the only teacher.

items.quote: A true Phisitian should be the minister, not a master to Nature
items.note: Restates the heading: the physician is Nature's minister.

items.name: Hippocrates & Galen
items.quote: a Philosopher skilfull to cure acording to the conclusion of Hippocrates & Galen
items.note: The physician as a philosopher skilled to cure is given as the conclusion of Hippocrates and Galen.

items.quote: others far more excellent and more truly deserving the name of Philosophers investigate the Arcana and more secret things of Nature
items.note: Two sects of philosophers: the vulgar look below the Moon at elementary nature; the better ones search out Nature's Arcana and secret things.

items.quote: they go into the very inner roomes and Sanctuary of Nature
items.note: Nature figured as a building with inner rooms and a sanctuary entered only by the true philosophers.

items.quote: A Physitian is compleated by 3 things
items.note: Announces three things that complete a physician; the list that follows names the natural virtue of growing things, the celestial influence causing it, its uniting by Chymistry with the firmament, and the physician's dexterity, so the count of items against '3' is not clear from the wording.

items.quote: the uniting of it by Chymistry with the Constellation of the firmament
items.note: A step of work: the earthly virtue is united by chymistry with the constellation of the firmament.

items.quote: Many errours of the Ancients are discovered by dayly experience, which yet hath not attained its end neither.
items.note: Experience uncovers the ancients' errors but is itself not complete.

items.name: Paracelsus
items.quote: as Paracelsus saith, let him be the legetimate INTERPRETER of NATURE
items.note: The first requirement of the physician is given in Paracelsus' words.

items.quote: let him be the legetimate INTERPRETER of NATURE
items.note: Set in capitals and numbered 'first' (followed by 'Secondly' in CH5.12): the physician's first qualification; he searches out all creatures and then considers man.

items.name: Chirurgia magna
items.quote: In Chirurgia magna.
items.note: The margin names the writing of Paracelsus the CH5.8 saying comes from.

items.quote: Phylosophy and Astronomy make a perfect Phylosopher, not onely in the great, but also in the little world.
items.note: Philosophy (earth and water) and Astronomy (fire and air) together make the perfect philosopher in both great and little world.

items.quote: Phylosophy teacheth the vertues and qualityes of the Earth and Water, as Astronomy doth of the fire and Ayre
items.note: The text defines Phylosophy and Astronomy by the elements each covers.

items.quote: Chyromancy, Pyromancy and Geomancy are the Elements of Astronomy and Phylosophy.
items.note: These three arts are named as the elements of Astronomy and Philosophy, which a physician should know.

items.quote: from the knowledge of Heaven and Earth, whose Nature and quality he doth perfectly understand
items.note: The true philosopher has his origin in knowledge of heaven and earth; the note also says philosophy rises in admiration (partly illegible).

items.quote: Theophrasteans contemplate and admire the workmanship of Nature throughout this mighty frame of the whole Creation
items.note: The followers of Theophrastus are named as a group and their study described.

items.quote: a wise inquisition into the qualities, affections, motions, courses and recourses of the Heavens and fiery bodies
items.note: Their work: inquiry into the heavens, their motions, and the seeds and principles of sublunary bodies, with observation and diligence.

items.quote: they doe at last attaine not onely to understand, but also really to imitate the greatest mysteries and secrets of Nature
items.note: By study, meditation and prayer the Theophrasteans come to understand and imitate Nature's mysteries and secrets, and to use them.

items.quote: By this meditation, which is a frequent cogitation
items.note: The margin defines meditation as frequent cogitation, by which the cause and reason of every thing is found.

items.quote: the Physitian begins to move and proceed in the Analogicall Concordance of the Naturall Light of the Microcosm with that of the great world
items.note: Where the philosopher stops at the Macrocosm, the physician continues by the analogy between Microcosm and great world.

items.quote: Secondly, a Physitian must be a good SPAGIRUS
items.note: The second qualification of the physician, set in capitals.

items.quote: one that can seperate the pure from the impure
items.note: The text says what a SPAGIRUS is: one who separates pure from impure.

items.quote: restore his Patient to health by a wise Alchymicall preparation
items.note: Healing done by alchymical preparation.

items.quote: As Gold is tryed seven times in the fire
items.note: Comparison: the physician is to be proved by Chymistry as gold is tried in fire.

items.quote: Chymistry, which sepereteth the good from the bad
items.note: Chymistry defined by its work of separating good from bad.

items.quote: Phylosophy is a practicall Physicke helping the Physitian to any medicine in a readynesse
items.note: Here philosophy is called a practical physic.

items.quote: he it is who at length becomes a good Physitian, born of the Light of Nature, to whom Nature communicateth his Experience
items.note: The good physician is born of the Light of Nature and taught by Nature's experience.

items.quote: never was there any man that ever knew and publisht such hard and hidden secrets in all Phylosophy and Physicke
items.note: Paracelsus is said to have known and published hidden secrets beyond anyone.

items.quote: the true Monarch of Physicke, and first Physitian of man
items.note: Croll's praise of Paracelsus as unequalled.

items.quote: hath written of the Internall Astrall Man and the service which God created him for
items.note: Paracelsus alone since Noe is said to have written of the Internal Astral Man and of the natural and metaphysical origin of great diseases.

items.quote: so that, as hath been said, they have taken no notice of that twofold unknown body of the Creatures
items.note: 'as hath been said' points back to an earlier place in the writing where the twofold body was discussed.

items.quote: that Mortall, Elementated Physicall and visible Corporeall body of the Elements; and the Astrall Sydereal and invisible of the Firmament and the stars
items.note: The two bodies of the creatures are named: the visible elemental body and the invisible astral, sidereal body.

items.quote: A Philosopher and Physitian spring one out of another, are the root of each other, the onely Spagyrick cook of all things.
items.note: Philosopher and physician arise from each other.

items.quote: Phylosophy is the mother of Physitians
items.note: Philosophy named as the mother of physicians; the rest of the note is largely illegible.

items.quote: The Intellectuall Soul of Man, that divine Light flowing out of that spiracle of God and Divine springs pertaineth to the Invisible Phylosophy, whose foundation is CHRIST
items.note: The intellectual soul belongs to an Invisible Philosophy founded on Christ.

items.quote: Our study therefore and profession of Phylosophy should be Christian-like, not after the manner of the Heathen in hollow empty language and temporaneous Arts
items.note: Philosophy should be Christian, not heathen.

items.quote: this is true Theologicall Phylosophy
items.note: Knowing nature and, by the Light of Grace, possessing eternal life with Christ is named true Theological Philosophy.

items.quote: Wherefore the New Birth is first to be sought for, and then all other Naturall things will be added without much labour.
items.note: The New Birth comes first; natural things follow easily.

items.quote: the Fundamentall of Faith and new Regeneration or Celestiall Transplantation
items.note: Regeneration is glossed as Celestial Transplantation; by it all sciences are attained.

items.quote: A man cannot have better Phylosophy then f{G162: 1 letter illegible}om God in the Regeneration.
items.note: The best philosophy comes from God in the Regeneration.

items.quote: But let us return againe to Theophrastus.
items.note: Marks a return to Theophrastus after the passage on Christian philosophy.

items.quote: He was a man singularly well skild in Chymistry, though he were not the Auther of that Art
items.note: Paracelsus was skilled in chymistry but did not originate it.

items.quote: from whom Paracelsus hath secretly borrowed many things
items.note: Paracelsus is said to have borrowed secretly from earlier philosophers famous in the art.

items.quote: There have been abundance of Phylosophers who have made use of there ingenuity and memory instead of bookes
items.note: Many earlier philosophers were famous in the art before Paracelsus, sitting uneasily beside CH5.12, which says none ever knew and published such secrets and no man ever attained his skill.

items.quote: For that noble Pyronomicall Art hath been most ancient
items.note: Chymistry named as the Pyronomical Art and called most ancient.

items.quote: which heretofore was known only to Kings Princes, & some few of most diligent searchers out of Naturall Phylosophy
items.note: The art was formerly known only to a few.

items.quote: the True and Philosophicall Physick which none in his time assayed to restore
items.note: The ancient doctrine, lost for many years, is named the True and Philosophical Physic, which Paracelsus sought to restore.

items.quote: the great obscurity of which art he laboured also to evolve and illustrate
items.note: The art is obscure; Paracelsus worked to unfold it and purge it of imposture.

items.quote: by a kind of divine copulation from the compasse of the whole circle unto the one only Centre
items.note: Figure of circle and centre for drawing all sciences back into one.

items.quote: hath stirred up his Emissaries and catch-poles
items.note: The Devil is said to have stirred up opponents of this truth.

items.quote: This kind of Phylosophy hath been in good esteem among many Nations.
items.note: Margin on the antiquity and esteem of this philosophy.

items.quote: all wonders, mysteries and secrets are to be attributed to God
items.note: Wonders and secrets come from God, not the Devil, creatures or stars; the note cites James 1.17.

items.quote: The Physitian that God maketh can doe all things.
items.note: The God-made physician's power.

items.quote: who by peculiar influence was born a Physitian
items.note: Theophrastus was born a physician by a particular influence; his gifts came from God.

items.quote: thus they make the Devill stonger then the blessed and glorious God
items.note: Croll charges the opponents who ascribe Paracelsus' cures to the Devil with impiety.

items.quote: the Devill, who hath no power over the Will and Understanding of Man
items.note: The Devil has no power over man's will and understanding.

items.quote: by a malicious ignorance obscuring his Wisdome or hidden Image in Man
items.note: God's wisdom is called a hidden image in man, which the opponents obscure.

items.quote: to contemn those Secrets which God hath granted to their Nature
items.note: German physicians wrong their own country by despising native secrets and preferring foreign ones.

items.quote: For as the Aristotelians unworthily rose up and set themselves against him, even so doe the mingle mangle Physitians against Theophrastus Paracelsus
items.note: Parallel: Aristotelians against Ramus, physicians against Paracelsus.

items.name: Paracels.
items.quote: See Paracels. de Fundamento Sa{G164: 1 letter illegible}ientia.
items.note: The margin points the reader to writings of Paracelsus, also naming one 'Corda'.

items.quote: He that doth not carelesly read but inwardly examine his writings will perceive as much.
items.note: Paracelsus' writings must be examined inwardly, not read carelessly, to be understood.

items.quote: he onely is able to judge of Truth who is inspired with Divine Wisdome
items.note: Only the divinely inspired can judge truth, so opponents cannot judge Paracelsus' Divinity.

items.quote: that invincible united Fundamentall of Theologicall and Phylosophicall Truth and perfect Piety
items.what: that invincible united Fundamentall of Theologicall and Phylosophicall Truth and perfect Piety
items.note: Names what Paracelsus' divine writings tried to make known.

items.quote: taken out of the Book of Grace and Nature, that is, that our mind should be raised up to God
items.note: 'that is' explains the Fundamental: raising the mind to God and seeking blessedness through Regeneration.

items.quote: in Physick as the Soule in the body.
items.note: Divinity should dwell in physic as the soul in the body.

items.quote: Numen & Lumen, Divine Power and Light, these two make a perfect Man.
items.note: The Latin pair is glossed as Divine Power and Light.

items.quote: By meditating or contemplating we know, by knowing we are delighted, by delighting we adhere, by adhearing we possesse, by possessing we injoy the Truth
items.what: meditating, knowing, delighting, adhering, possessing, enjoying
items.note: A graded series of steps from meditation to enjoying truth.

items.name: Div. Dionys.
items.quote: Read Div. Dionys.
items.note: The margin refers the reader to Dionysius and Picus Mirandula.

items.quote: Without Phylosophy it is impossible to be absolutely godly
items.note: Philosophy and godliness need each other.

items.quote: The two Lights are well known, within which are all thing, without which is nothing
items.note: Names the two Lights, of Grace and of Nature.

items.quote: The Light of Nature, which is the Treasury of God confirmed in the Scriptures, maketh a true Phylosopher
items.note: Light of Nature defined as God's treasury; Light of Grace makes the theologer.

items.quote: The works of God are bipactite; Philosophy comprehendeth the works or way of Nature; Theologie onely knoweth the works and way of Christ
items.note: God's works are twofold; philosophy and theology each take one.

items.quote: every true Theologer is a Phylosopher, and every true Phylosopher is a Theologer
items.note: The two callings coincide.

items.quote: such as Paulus Brawn of Norimberge, Valentinus Weigelius, and Petrus Winzius
items.what: Paulus Brawn of Norimberge, Valentinus Weigelius, and Petrus Winzius
items.note: Successors of Paracelsus in this study are named.

items.quote: not in the sensuall school of fools, nor in the rationall school of Schollers, but in the third school of perfect Men, that Mentall or Intellectuall school of Pentecost
items.what: the third school of perfect Men
items.note: Three schools are distinguished: sensual, rational, and the mental school of Pentecost.

items.quote: by the favour nf the most High will in their time come to Light, unlesse the indignity and ingratitude of the world keep them back
items.note: The manuscripts of these men are not yet public and are to come to light in their time.

items.quote: the annihilation, abnegation, immolation and mortification of themselves by Christ
items.note: Inward steps: self-mortification, casting off shadows, turning into the Temple of the heart, daily practice of piety.

items.quote: that huge Talent and Treasury which is hid and shut up within themselvs
items.note: A treasury lies hidden within the reader, to be fetched out by piety.

items.quote: should in vaine seek those things without them by many books, mortall masters, long journeys
items.note: Outward seeking through books and masters is vain.

items.quote: the whole Animall Man, who is nothing but EARTH
items.note: The Animal Man is defined as nothing but earth.

items.name: David
items.quote: entred into themselves with David, Psal. 40 1.
items.note: David and the Psalms are cited for the inward waiting on God.

items.quote: the very determinate and appointed End of the Cabala or secret wisdome
items.note: Cabala glossed as secret wisdom; its end is God working all our works in us.

items.quote: Christ is to be found in the Temple of the Heart.
items.note: Margin repeats the inward search.

items.quote: God is to be waited for with a quiet mind when the sences are laid asleep
items.note: Waiting on God with the senses quieted.

items.quote: The heart of a Regenerate man is Gods Eden or Garden of Pleasure, wherein he dwelleth
items.note: The regenerate heart is called God's Eden.

items.quote: though now he is not discerned by reason of the Dark Point of the Quaternary
items.note: Number language whose sense these lines do not explain.

items.quote: at the end of this world which is to be Renewed by the Ternary of Man
items.note: Ternary of Man, set against the Quaternary; glossed by Soul, Spirit, and Body.

items.quote: the Regeneration according to Soul, Spirit, and Body (the New Jerusalem
items.note: The Regeneration of soul, spirit and body is called the New Jerusalem.

items.quote: will sparkle and glitter out with a radiant fiery colour like a Rubie or Carbuncle thorow the clear, spotlesse, beautifull body
items.note: Image of the renewed body shining red like a ruby or carbuncle.

items.quote: where Mans Left hand knoweth not what Gods Right hand doth
items.note: Figure for God working in the man unseen by him.

items.name: Apoc.
items.note: The margin names the writing beside the New Jerusalem passage.

items.quote: all is vanity but to love God and cleave to him by serving him alone
items.note: Only love of God is not vanity.

items.quote: so inevitably fall back into that vaine, wicked or our own Nothing
items.note: Self-love leads back into our own Nothing.

items.quote: The Fall of Man and our great evill is to depart from Unity to Alterity.
items.note: The Fall defined as departing from Unity to Alterity.

items.name: Seneca
items.quote: I never go abroad among men but I come home lesse a man then when I went forth
items.note: Seneca quoted in the margin.

items.quote: If the Soule run back within it selfe and be converted into the Mind it draweth near to God, seeth all things, and hath no need of outward teaching
items.note: The soul turned inward knows all without outward teaching; turned to sense it departs from God.

items.quote: The Academicall spirit cannot not understand this Mystery
items.note: A mystery closed to the academic spirit; only humility is capable of illumination.

items.quote: nor may I in this unfit place openly speak more of these Mysteries
items.note: Croll withholds further speech on these mysteries here.

items.quote: I returne againe to that Physitian Paracelsus from the digression unto which I had occasion to step aside
items.note: Marks CH5.13 onward material as a digression and returns to Paracelsus.

items.quote: O what pains doe they take to become sools, who once drown themselves in Humane wisdome.
items.note: Margin against human wisdom.

items.quote: using such words which every one doth not understand
items.note: Paracelsus is hated for words not everyone understands.

items.quote: tis easier to carp at him then to imitate him
items.note: Critics carp instead of imitating; the margin N214 gives a foreign-script version with 'facilius. quam'.

items.quote: the malicious ingratitude of men may be the cause of the bewayled obscurity of his Commentators
items.note: Obscurity of Paracelsus' commentators is excused by men's ingratitude.

items.quote: the unusuall custome of Phylosophers plead for the strange novelties of names
items.note: Strange names are defended as the philosophers' custom.

items.quote: the Phylosophers have ever driven from their hives of most sacred Sciences those sluggish and lazy Drones
items.note: Philosophers keep the lazy out of their sciences, a reason for obscurity.

items.name: Plato
items.quote: Arts wrapt in Riddles safe doe lye
items.note: Introduced in CH5.25 by 'as Plato saith'.

items.quote: Their fruitfull'st soyle is Secrecy.
items.note: Arts thrive in secrecy and riddles.

items.name: Plato
items.quote: Artes ut lateant sua perque Aenigmata crescunt.
items.note: Latin of the verse in CH5.26.

items.quote: A man may live any where, Lawes and Liberties are alowed in every Dominion
items.note: Opening of the paragraph; its link to what follows is not explained in these lines.

items.quote: if he had that which Theophrastus knew, whether he would tell it to every man
items.note: Knowledge like Theophrastus' is not to be told to everyone.

items.name: Hippocrates
items.quote: he would break the Oath of Hippocrates, who would not instruct every one in the Art of Physick
items.note: The Oath of Hippocrates cited for withholding the art from all comers.
